title: HelioCRM x Redwood — SDK retries + streaming reliability follow-up
next_steps: Redwood to share TS SDK patch release ETA and changelog snippet (retry defaults + respect Retry-After).
Customer to provide a 10–15 minute window of request-ids covering the 429 burst to correlate gateway logs.
Redwood to share guidance on per-service retry configuration (max attempts / retry budget) for HelioCRM’s worker services.
Schedule a short follow-up after TS patch lands to confirm 429 behavior and no retry amplification.
body:
Fireflies.ai — Transcript

Meeting: HelioCRM x Redwood — SDK retries + streaming reliability follow-up
Date: 2025-01-16
Start time: 09:00 PT
Duration: 46 minutes

Attendees
Redwood Inference: Dev Patel, Ibrahim Khan, Dana Lo, Rafael Mendes
HelioCRM: Maya Thompson, Jon Park, Elena García, Priya Nair

Summary (auto-generated)
- HelioCRM escalated inconsistent retry behavior between Redwood Python SDK and TypeScript SDK across multiple services.
- Primary impact: TS services retried aggressively on 429s leading to longer throttling windows and elevated spend; Python services behaved differently (fewer retries / different timeouts), causing uneven user experience.
- Redwood confirmed ongoing cross-SDK parity work and discussed near-term mitigation (config overrides) plus upcoming patch releases.

Topics (auto-generated)
- 429 handling and honoring Retry-After
- Retry budgets vs max attempts, jitter/backoff alignment
- Request-id correlation and observability signals
- Rollout plan for TS + Python patch versions

Action items (auto-generated)
- Dev Patel: email HelioCRM the interim TS retry configuration snippet and recommended defaults for background workers by EOD 2025-01-16.
- Dana Lo: confirm whether current TS release uses per-request retry budget correctly for streaming vs non-streaming, and report back by 2025-01-17.
- Jon Park: send request-id samples + timestamps from the incident window by 2025-01-17.
- Rafael Mendes: provide SRE guidance on safe retry limits for 429 burst patterns and queue workers by 2025-01-20.

Transcript

[00:00] Dev Patel: Alright, I think we’re good. Thanks everybody for hopping on. Maya, you had flagged the inconsistent retries between TypeScript and Python, and it sounded like it became kind of an incident for you all.

[00:14] Maya Thompson: Yeah, incident-ish. Not an outage, but we had like, a degraded day. Our Node services basically kept hammering the API after 429s. The Python service did something different and that actually masked it for a while.

[00:28] Ibrahim Khan: Got it. Maybe we start with your architecture just to make sure we’re talking about the same pieces.

[00:33] Jon Park: Sure. We have two main callers. One is a Node/TypeScript “conversation” service, synchronous path, user-facing. Then we have Python workers that do summarization and embeddings async. Both talk to Redwood Hosted API.

[00:48] Elena García: And we have Envoy in front of the Node service, and then Python workers go through our egress NAT. Different network paths, but same Redwood org, same API keys.

[01:02] Dev Patel: Helpful. And the symptom was what exactly—like request volume exploded, or latency, or both?

[01:09] Elena García: Both. Latency spiked first. Then 429s started. The TS service kept retrying—like immediately. We saw our own queue depth blow up and the throttling window got worse. It felt like a feedback loop.

[01:26] Priya Nair: From product, the user-facing chat got inconsistent. Some users would see a response after like 40 seconds, others would fail. Meanwhile the async jobs still completed, so it was like half the system looked fine.

[01:40] Dana Lo: Okay. On TS: were you using the default client config, or did you customize retries?

[01:46] Jon Park: Default. We set a timeout but not retries. I think we assumed “reasonable defaults.”

[01:54] Ibrahim Khan: Totally fair. That’s essentially why we’re doing this parity project. We found that defaults diverged, especially around 429 and how to treat Retry-After.

[02:06] Maya Thompson: To be blunt, the TS default behavior is not reasonable for enterprise traffic. It felt like it ignored rate limiting.

[02:14] Dana Lo: Understood. And sorry—yeah. Let me ask a couple specifics. When you got the 429s, do you have headers captured? Specifically, did you see Retry-After or request-id?

[02:26] Elena García: We have request-id in logs. For Retry-After, I’m not 100% sure. We can check. Our log line includes response headers but it’s sampled.

[02:36] Dev Patel: If you can share even a couple request-ids from the burst window, we can correlate on our side and confirm what we were emitting.

[02:44] Jon Park: Yeah, we have a whole list. We pulled like 200 request IDs. We can send a small subset.

[02:51] Rafael Mendes: And just to frame it: for 429, safe behavior is generally “respect Retry-After if present, otherwise back off with jitter and a budget.” If you retry immediately, you basically amplify the storm.

[03:04] Maya Thompson: That’s exactly what happened.

[03:07] Ibrahim Khan: What did Python do during that same window?

[03:11] Jon Park: Python workers were slower, so they didn’t spike as hard. Also, I think the Python client had fewer retries? But then we saw some jobs “hang” longer than expected. Might be timeouts.

[03:23] Dev Patel: Okay, so we have two issues: TS retry aggression on 429, and Python timeouts/behavior being different so your systems don’t fail uniformly.

[03:33] Dana Lo: On TS, we recently changed some retry internals because Node runtimes vary (fetch vs undici). There may be a bug where we’re treating 429 as retryable but not applying the full exponential backoff, and not honoring Retry-After consistently.

[03:49] Maya Thompson: Is that already fixed, or…

[03:51] Dana Lo: It’s in progress. We have a patch queued that aligns to the new cross-SDK retry spec. I can’t promise a date in this call but we can give a timeline.

[04:02] Ibrahim Khan: The standard we’re rolling out is: 429 is retryable, but only with capped attempts and a retry budget, and it should honor Retry-After. Also jitter is required.

[04:13] Elena García: Can you define “retry budget”? Because we use Envoy too, and we don’t want stacked retries.

[04:18] Rafael Mendes: Yeah. Budget meaning you cap total time spent retrying (or total attempts) per request, and ideally you instrument it. For example: “do not spend more than 8 seconds retrying on 429/503 combined” and do not exceed, say, 2 or 3 retries for user-facing.

[04:35] Dev Patel: And we’ll recommend different defaults for user-facing vs background workers.

[04:39] Priya Nair: Right now it’s user-facing that hurts most.

[04:42] Ibrahim Khan: Exactly. For synchronous chat, you’d rather fail fast and let the user retry, versus retrying internally for 45 seconds.

[04:52] Jon Park: Our TS service currently sets a 60-second timeout. Which is probably too high.

[04:56] Dana Lo: For chat streaming, long overall timeouts can be okay if the stream is active, but your client needs read timeouts that don’t kill an active stream, and you still need sane retry semantics.

[05:08] Dev Patel: Quick check: are you streaming responses from Node?

[05:12] Jon Park: Yes, for chat. We stream tokens.

[05:16] Dana Lo: Okay. Then one important point: we do not recommend retrying mid-stream disconnects automatically as if it’s idempotent, because you can duplicate output or double-charge tokens. We have a policy for that.

[05:31] Maya Thompson: Good, because that was another thing. We saw duplicates in a few traces. Not sure if it was us or the SDK.

[05:37] Dana Lo: It can happen if your application restarts the request after receiving partial output and you don’t dedupe, or if a proxy buffers and then disconnects. We’re tightening the TS streaming cancel/disconnect handling too.

[05:50] Ibrahim Khan: Today’s focus though: the 429 retries. Let’s dig into numbers. Elena, when the burst happened, what was your RPS approximately?

[05:58] Elena García: Peak around 120 requests/sec from the Node service. That’s higher than normal; we had a product launch email.

[06:07] Rafael Mendes: If the client retries even once per request quickly, you can double or triple that instantly.

[06:13] Dev Patel: And did you see 503s too, or mostly 429?

[06:17] Elena García: Mostly 429. A few 5xx but the dominant was rate limiting.

[06:23] Dana Lo: That matches what we’ve seen in other cases. If we ignore Retry-After, we create the exact bad loop.

[06:30] Maya Thompson: So what’s the remediation? We can’t wait weeks.

[06:35] Dev Patel: Totally. We have two tracks. Immediate: you can override TS retry settings now to reduce retries on 429, and/or honor Retry-After at the app layer if you’re catching the error.

[06:46] Jon Park: We didn’t see a clean error type. It’s like a generic “API error.”

[06:50] Dana Lo: That’s also in scope. Error taxonomy should expose status code, request-id, and retry-after if present.

[06:58] Ibrahim Khan: But for immediate mitigation, we can send a snippet: set maxRetries to 0 for streaming endpoints and maxRetries to 1 or 2 for non-streaming, with a cap. That will stop the storm.

[07:11] Maya Thompson: Are you basically saying “turn off retries” until you fix it?

[07:14] Rafael Mendes: For user-facing streaming, yes—generally. For non-streaming POSTs, you can do limited retries on safe conditions, but 429 needs to be treated carefully.

[07:24] Elena García: What about GET requests? Do you even have GETs here?

[07:27] Ibrahim Khan: Most of the inference calls are POST. We treat them as non-idempotent by default. We rely on request IDs for correlation, not for replay.

[07:36] Dev Patel: On patch timeline: the TS patch that aligns 429 behavior is planned as a patch release, not a major. We’re targeting early next week for publish, assuming final testing passes.

[07:49] Maya Thompson: Early next week meaning… Monday? Wednesday?

[07:52] Dana Lo: Realistically Tuesday or Wednesday. I want to be careful. We have conformance tests we’re running across Node versions.

[08:00] Jon Park: Okay.

[08:02] Dev Patel: For Python, you also mentioned “hang.” That might be timeouts. Python currently has different default timeouts than TS, and it can appear like it’s stuck if the read timeout is too long and you’re behind a buffering proxy.

[08:16] Elena García: Our Python workers aren’t streaming. They do normal responses. But they run behind Celery and we saw tasks exceeding expected runtime.

[08:25] Ibrahim Khan: Then it might be retries + long overall timeouts combining. Or it could be connect timeouts. We’d need specific logs.

[08:32] Jon Park: We can pull one example. But the main pain is TS.

[08:36] Priya Nair: Yeah, we need the user-facing path stable.

[08:40] Dana Lo: Can I ask—are you using any client-side concurrency limiting? Like a semaphore or queue for the Node service.

[08:46] Jon Park: We do, but it’s pretty loose. We allow bursts.

[08:50] Rafael Mendes: Bursts plus aggressive retries is the worst combination. Even after we patch, I’d recommend adding an upper bound on in-flight requests to your chat endpoint.

[09:02] Maya Thompson: That’s fair. But we still expect the SDK to not be dangerous by default.

[09:07] Ibrahim Khan: Agreed. The design goal is “safe by default.” We’re codifying that now.

[09:14] Dev Patel: Let’s talk specifics for your config. Jon, what library version are you on for TS?

[09:19] Jon Park: Redwood SDK TS 1.7.2. I can confirm but pretty sure.

[09:23] Dana Lo: Okay. The patch will likely be 1.7.3 or 1.7.4 depending on sequencing. It will change default retry classifier and backoff.

[09:33] Maya Thompson: Will that be breaking?

[09:35] Dana Lo: It’s behavior change, but it’s in the direction of fewer retries / safer. Some people might have relied on retries, but we think this is the right default.

[09:44] Ibrahim Khan: And we’ll document it as a behavior change in release notes and migration guidance.

[09:50] Elena García: Are you going to expose metrics hooks? Because we need to see retry counts per request.

[09:55] Dev Patel: We have optional telemetry hooks in the standard. It might not land in the first patch, but it’s in-flight. In the short term, you can log the request-id and status plus attempt number.

[10:07] Dana Lo: The patch should at minimum include: (1) attempt count, (2) request-id surfaced, (3) respect Retry-After.

[10:17] Jon Park: Respecting Retry-After is huge. Right now we just see it immediately retry.

[10:23] Rafael Mendes: And jitter. Without jitter, everybody lines up again.

[10:27] Dana Lo: Yep.

[10:29] Dev Patel: Maya, can you share what you saw in terms of spacing? Like were retries happening in under 100ms?

[10:35] Maya Thompson: Some of them looked like 0ms, honestly. Like back-to-back.

[10:39] Dana Lo: That sounds like a bug in how we’re scheduling backoff when the runtime reports a certain error shape. I’ve seen something like that with undici.

[10:49] Ibrahim Khan: That’s consistent with what we’re auditing—different Node runtimes surface network errors differently, and the retry classifier ended up taking a fast path.

[11:00] Elena García: Another question: does Redwood gateway always return Retry-After on 429?

[11:05] Dev Patel: It should for most rate limit cases, but I don’t want to overpromise. We can confirm in logs. Platform has been improving payload consistency as well.

[11:15] Ibrahim Khan: The spec assumes: if Retry-After is present, honor it. If not, backoff exponentially with jitter, and still cap.

[11:25] Priya Nair: What about when we get 503? Same behavior?

[11:28] Rafael Mendes: 503 is retryable in limited fashion. But for user-facing streaming, again, you don’t want to “silently retry” because you can duplicate user-visible output.

[11:40] Dana Lo: For non-streaming 503/504, limited retries with budget is okay.

[11:45] Jon Park: Our streaming is SSE. Does the SDK parse the events correctly? We sometimes saw partial frames.

[11:52] Dana Lo: That’s in another patch line. But today I want to keep the scope on 429 storm.

[12:00] Dev Patel: Here’s what I propose: (1) immediate config change today for TS: set retries to 0 for streaming, 1 for non-streaming; (2) we deliver patch early next week; (3) you test in staging with a synthetic 429 burst and confirm it backs off.

[12:16] Maya Thompson: Okay. Can you send the config snippet after this call? We need it ASAP.

[12:19] Dev Patel: Yes. I’ll email it today.

[12:22] Elena García: And I’ll send request IDs.

[12:25] Dev Patel: Great.

[12:27] Ibrahim Khan: Also, one more thing: do you set your own headers? Like idempotency keys or request IDs?

[12:34] Jon Park: We set a correlation ID header, but not sure it propagates.

[12:38] Dana Lo: The SDK should propagate a request-id returned from Redwood in response headers. For request correlation, we can also accept your header, but the key thing is logging the Redwood request-id.

[12:49] Elena García: We log it, but it wasn’t always present.

[12:53] Dev Patel: That could be because some failures happen before headers—like connection errors. But for 429 it should be present.

[13:02] Rafael Mendes: If you can share a couple raw HTTP captures, even sanitized, that would help.

[13:07] Maya Thompson: We can’t share full payloads. Security.

[13:10] Dev Patel: Totally. Just headers and status codes, no prompts.

[13:14] Maya Thompson: That’s fine.

[13:16] (crosstalk)

[13:17] Priya Nair: Are we going to get any credits for the extra spend during the storm?

[13:21] Dev Patel: I can’t approve credits on this call, but I can loop in your account owner. If it’s clearly caused by client retry behavior, we can review.

[13:30] Maya Thompson: Appreciate it.

[13:33] Ibrahim Khan: While we have SRE here, Rafael, can you give concrete numbers we recommend for chat streaming?

[13:40] Rafael Mendes: Sure. For chat streaming: retries on 429 should generally be 0. If you want to “retry” at the product layer, do it with user feedback and a delay, not hidden. For non-streaming completion calls: max 2 retries, exponential backoff starting at 250ms with full jitter, and a total budget like 4–8 seconds.

[14:02] Elena García: That’s helpful.

[14:04] Dana Lo: That’s basically what we’re setting as defaults in the standard. TS is currently not conforming.

[14:11] Jon Park: For the patch, can we get a pre-release build? Like a GitHub tag?

[14:16] Dana Lo: Potentially. If we cut an RC, we can share it. But it may be easier to give you a branch commit hash. Are you okay consuming that?

[14:24] Maya Thompson: We can do a commit hash in staging.

[14:27] Dev Patel: Okay, Dana, can you share that once you have it.

[14:31] Dana Lo: Yes.

[14:33] Dev Patel: And from our side, we want to make sure your configuration is not stacking with Envoy retries. Elena, does Envoy also retry 429?

[14:41] Elena García: No, we disabled 429 retries at Envoy. It retries on connect failures and some 5xx.

[14:48] Rafael Mendes: Good.

[14:50] Ibrahim Khan: That’s important. We’ve seen customers double retry.

[14:56] Maya Thompson: Another thing: Python service didn’t retry and that actually was “better” during the storm. But then it failed more quickly in other cases.

[15:06] Ibrahim Khan: Yep, that’s the flip side. The goal is consistent behavior, not “one retries a ton and the other never does.”

[15:14] Dev Patel: We’re going to align all three SDKs (Python/TS/Go). This call is focused on TS because it’s hurting you now.

[15:22] Priya Nair: If we change retries to zero, does that affect perceived reliability? Like more errors.

[15:28] Rafael Mendes: You might see more surfaced 429s, but it’s honestly more honest. And your system will recover faster because you’re not prolonging the throttling.

[15:38] Maya Thompson: Yeah, I’d rather show a “try again” than spin.

[15:42] Jon Park: Same.

[15:44] Dev Patel: Great. Let’s capture incident window details. Elena, what time range?

[15:49] Elena García: 10:20 to 11:05 UTC yesterday.

[15:53] Dev Patel: Perfect.

[15:55] Dana Lo: I want to validate something: are you on Node 18 or 20?

[16:00] Jon Park: Node 18 in prod. Node 20 in dev.

[16:03] Dana Lo: Okay. We’ll test both.

[16:06] Ibrahim Khan: Alright. We’re at ~16 minutes. Anything else on retries before we jump to timeline?

[16:12] Maya Thompson: Timeline is key.

[16:14] Dev Patel: Okay. Dana’s team is aiming for Tuesday/Wednesday patch for TS. Python patch is in progress but not required for your immediate incident. We’ll also send interim config today.

[16:26] Maya Thompson: And you’ll send the commit hash if possible.

[16:28] Dana Lo: Yes.

[16:29] Dev Patel: Great.

[16:31] (short pause)

[16:33] Priya Nair: Can we talk about how to communicate this internally? Like, we’ll change SDK behavior and our app might show more “rate limited” errors.

[16:42] Dev Patel: Yeah. We can share recommended UX patterns. But basically: show a quick message, back off, maybe allow user to retry.

[16:50] Rafael Mendes: And if you have a queue, enqueue and retry later rather than immediate.

[16:56] Maya Thompson: For chat, we probably just show an error.

[17:00] Dev Patel: Makes sense.

[17:02] Jon Park: One more detail: we saw some requests that did succeed after many retries, but then tokens were billed multiple times? It’s hard to tell.

[17:12] Dev Patel: If the request actually ran multiple times, yes, it can bill multiple times. That’s why retries on non-idempotent requests must be bounded and careful.

[17:21] Ibrahim Khan: We’re adding clearer docs around this.

[17:26] Maya Thompson: Okay.

[17:27] Dana Lo: On TS, we also will include a header to help you debug attempts—like “x-redwood-retry-attempt” or similar. Not sure if it’s in the patch.

[17:38] Dev Patel: We can follow up. Platform is also improving rate-limit error payload consistency.

[17:45] Elena García: Payload consistency would help because currently our parser can’t extract limit/reset.

[17:51] Dev Patel: Yep.

[17:52] (crosstalk)

[17:54] Ibrahim Khan: Okay, I think we have the key items. Let’s do a quick recap.

[18:00] Ibrahim Khan: Redwood will send you an interim TS config today: retries disabled for streaming, limited retries for non-streaming with backoff. You will send request-id samples and a header-only capture if possible. Dana will share an RC commit hash as soon as it’s ready, and target a patch release early next week. Rafael will send safe retry guidance numbers for your worker vs user-facing services.

[18:23] Maya Thompson: Sounds right.

[18:25] Dev Patel: Great. We’ll schedule a 20-minute follow-up next week after you test. Anything else before we drop?

[18:32] Priya Nair: No, thanks.

[18:34] Jon Park: Thanks.

[18:35] Elena García: Thank you.

[18:36] Dev Patel: Alright, talk soon.

(Transcript ends — remaining time contained small talk / dropped participants; Fireflies stopped capturing cleanly around minute ~19.)
